I live in a nice building, in an ostensibly nice neighborhood, in an ostensibly nice city.

Despite this, whenever I go outside I am confronted by unstable mentally ill and/or drug using people.

In the nearby shops, the shelves are completely encased in glass — even for small things like a bag of chips, you need staff assistance.

Many of the retail establishments have armed guards, with guns and body armor. I'm not talking about banks, or secure facilities — I'm talking about the grocery store.

The *average* response time for a "Tier 1" 911 call is 20 minutes. And for many crimes, the police simply won't come at all. When I was the victim of a felony hit and run, the cops told me they wouldn't dispatch an officer; it wasn't serious enough.

Not far from me, a man high on drugs sexually assaulted half a dozen women in a city park; the police showed up about 45 minutes after the first call was received. By that point, the man had already been sudued by a group of bystanders.

The homicide clearance rate in my city is around 40%.

When I step outside, it is abundantly clear that I am on my own. The authorities are unlikely to solve a crime committed against me, much less prevent a crime from taking place.

So, I carry a gun now. I am licensed and trained. I practice every week. I didn't arrive at this point because I have some sort of fixation on gun culture. This is just a rational response to the fact that government has given up on protecting ordinary people where I live.

comments.name: John D Garcia
comments.body:
What ???

The article lists July cash totals, a close Michigan primary, May Pew unfavorability numbers, Cook toss-up ratings, and two New Hampshire polls within the margin of error as signs Democratic momentum may stall. The facts may be real, but the article does not show how much electoral weight each fact carries. July cash is not November spending. One Michigan primary does not establish national voter behavior. A small socialist bloc does not establish the Democratic Party’s national direction.

A stronger forecast needs evidence showing whether those risks actually move voters: fall spending by race, likely-voter polling in the toss-up Senate states, the size of the anti-El-Sayed vote, and evidence showing whether socialist messaging hurts Democrats outside safe seats. Without that comparison, the article does not show that fundraising concerns, the Michigan nomination fight, and ideological divisions outweigh voter dissatisfaction involving President Trump, the Iran war, tariffs, and living costs.

The weakness is not the individual facts. The weakness is the inference drawn from the collection. The article moves from a list of possible Democratic vulnerabilities to a broader forecast without showing how strongly those vulnerabilities affect the electorate or how those vulnerabilities compare with the political forces benefiting Democrats. The forecast therefore rests on an unweighed list rather than a demonstrated electoral effect.

Using the proverbial analogy of steering an ocean liner, changing course mid-voyage is not an easy or quick thing. Making substantial changes once the course is determined comes only at a great additional costs, fiscal, inertial, and in the court of public opinion.

My company didn't seem to accept the reality of climate change until objectively studying the evidence for a time, then became more proactive in mitigating its impact by decreasing coal-fired generation, building more natural gas-fueled power stations, and constructing/promoting renewables, which are now far less costly to build and operate than the coal-fired behemoths of the earlier paradigm. I read the Diary last week after the comments were closed, too late to share my thoughts on “Full Freezer” by Diane Garofalo, about the steaks she could not afford. 

It reminded me of a Met Diary story of my own that ran August 22, 2021, about another steak. Forgive this liberty I am taking to share an overdue coda to  “A T-Bone Rides the 1.”

In this comedy, an abandoned steak is inspiring both comments and revulsion from subway riders. It is inspected and rejected by a shirtless man, who eventually snatches it up moments before he dashes out of the train.

What I left out only occurred to me later: After the man ran out, and the subway doors closed, he stayed on the platform standing at that door with the next set of passengers.

His ride was not over. He was just reluctant, perhaps ashamed, to remain on the train with the free meal in view of fellow riders.

We may never know the motives of the butcher in last week’s story. When I read it, my thoughts went back to that small shirtless man who ran out of the 1 train.

This was an excellent essay, but it didn't mention some related research… which has shown that most species of animals can't understand a human pointing at something, regardless of the context or incentives. They will just stare at the person's finger. Only a few species may understand what the human is doing and shift their gaze to where the finger is pointing.

A related topic I read about recently, which hit me really hard, was that high IQ in itself means little without what the author called "executive intelligence". That involves deciding what to do or not to do with one's time, the ability to keep focusing on one task until it's complete, and so on.

Another topic that might be worth revisiting: for a long time it was assumed that "people domesticated wolves into dogs". But more recently it's been suggested that a subset of smarter wolves, hanging around the outskirts of a human encampment, actually domesticated themselves when they realized how advantageous the partnership might be. I suppose there's similar or analogous behavior in some humans.

I wonder if getting on buprenorphine might have given him the protection from overdose he needed while he matured enough to make better choices or to "run out the clock" as his family described. While the newest highly potent fentanyl analogue hitting the streets is worrisome, the real scandals are the lack of access to safe and effective treatment for opioid use disorder and the stigma that keeps patients and families from starting these medications when they do have access.

In 2014, the Supreme Court ruled in American Broadcasting Cos., Inc. v. Aereo, Inc. in favor of the broadcasters. That wasn’t the beginning of the end for cable companies, but in retrospect it feels like the end of the end.
Shortly before that, I could plug a coaxial cable into the wall and get great local reception. Then Time Warner wanted $45 a month just for local TV. Outrageous. Aereo offered essentially what I wanted for $8 a month, until the Supreme Court ruling shut that down.
So I bought an antenna. Some channels didn’t come in particularly well, but oh well.
Now it’s all about streaming, and the free streaming services offer plenty. I’ll subscribe to HBO to watch White Lotus or Apple to watch Severance, then cancel when I’m finished.
And how many people do you know who still have a home phone number they don’t need because it was bundled into the “triple play”?

I don't see why the museum doesn't just redefine what "Cable" is.  A lot of what constituted cable has been repackaged to streaming.  Part of cable is the constellation of cable stations that created the content.  Well much if not almost all of those stations now reach viewers via streaming services, and almost all are subsidiaries of streaming companies.  The other part of cable is the infrastructure, as in the physical cable and associated switches and nodes in the system.  Well, they still exist, but they are used to provide internet access.

The part of "Cable" that is diminished is the large packages, or tiers, of stations that pipe live TV into houses, often with advertisements.  To that part, I say good riddance.  I never appreciated having to pay for access to a wide range of stations, of which I only watched a few.  I also don't like linear TV, and how it makes you adjust your viewing to its schedule, not having control of when you watch what program or which episode of it.

An old friend used to say, if there's a TV program that you rarely watch.  If you only watch it twice, chances are it'll end up being the same episode.

In a way, this meeting shows the power of having a functionally powerless but highly prestigious monarchy.  British politicians and AI executives alike can hide behind King Charles' robes, while he himself walks a remarkable tightrope.  Everyone else is too afraid of Trump and thinks they might get fired or ruined, but the King cannot get fired.  Britain continually works the monarchy angle to get awkward things done.

“Perceived irrelevance” of opera. Many times perception is reality. 

Citing what the great Toscanini would do to save opera when he has been gone for over 50 years doesn’t really prove opera can be “saved”. It shows the place where opera exists now. A smaller slice of devotees and an art form which dwells in the past.

My 7th-grade choir teacher, Miss Triplett, taught us so much about opera and music generally.  Once she played "Un Bel Di, Vedremo" sung by two different sopranos, and had us vote on which one we preferred.  We voted for Renata Tebaldi and she approved.  No one said opera, yuck.  Of course, we mostly loved music already or we wouldn't have been in choir. 

I wonder whether my classmates went on to attend operas.  I've been to many and always think of Miss Triplett.

While people think opera may be in a fragile state, it is not dead by any means as demonstrated by Opera Phila. Good singers,  creative management, and attractive productions with reasonable ticket prices is a winning combination. We came away thinking that opera was alive and well, but you have to believe in it. I believe any American opera company can do this.

But I kept going and liked the lighter operas. In Seattle I kept going and learned to love Wagner, thanks to our wonderful director Speight Jenkins. It takes some exposure in a nice hall to really feel the power of this music. Try it and give it some time.

We all went to the film version of Carmen with Placido Domingo and the (very steamy) Julia Migenes-Johnson. The sons had been told the outline of the story beforehand, and they were absolutely transfixed through the entire movie. Afterwards we all had a great conversation about whether Carmen was an evil hussy or misunderstood. I would love to know if those boys went on to become operagoers, and if they introduced opera (and classical music) to their kids.

comments.name: Traitor To My Demographic
comments.body: Celine reminds this American of the many, many contributions made by Canadians to our common culture, going beyond the tabloid images of the debonair Pierre Elliott Trudeau jet-setting around with Bianca Jagger.  Our shared culture starts with Ice Hockey, of course, but it also flows from such diverse Canadian artists as Gordon Lightfoot, Sarah McLachlan, Anne Murray, Avril Lavigne, Joni Mitchell, Alanis Morissette, Shania Twain, the players of the Montreal Symphony, John Candy, Eugene Levy, Ryan Reynolds, Alice Munro, and of course many others.  But the magical thing about Celine is the window she gives us English speaking cousins in the US into French Canadian culture.  And that opens up a whole other area of interest, how Canadian artists have influenced the arts in other countries.  For example, Canadian author Gabrielle Roy was born in Manitoba (yep, not Quebec!), yet she is one of the most respected writers in the French language.  We’re lucky to have such amazing neighbors who are a lot like us, yet who are uniquely their own, too.

comments.name: AM
comments.body: Although I agree we need more focus in healthcare on menopause and its treatments, I would prefer an actual healthcare system that functions first. There is a whole subspecialty of reproductive endocrinology which could focus on menopause but focuses on IVF because it is a money maker. Universal healthcare with parity between medical specialties needs to be addressed first. A bunch of performative meetings about menopause doesn’t fix the underlying problem most people deal with, which is the cost and difficulty accessing healthcare.

comments.name: Brenda
comments.body:
I think this is a worthy idea, but I agree it might come out as out of touch/“woke,” especially by this administration. Some context might help. The government spends up to $84 million on ED drugs, primarily through DOD alone (not including Medicare). The vast majority of this is on veterans, not active duty. There is no figure on what, if anything the government spends on HRT. In 2007 (likely is more now), 17 percent of adult men had ED. (This could be misleading because it’s far more common as men age) By this estimate, 33 percent of women have adverse menopausal symptoms, although virtually all women will go through menopause. Since most women have severest symptoms before Medicare, the government probably spends very little in healthcare for women going through menopause. 

I’m not saying that ED and HRT are apples to apples issues or that expenditures should be comparable, but it’s instructive that there appears to be no figure on menopause issues and research but easily found figures for ED, while both issues affect all aging adults at various times.

Nor would I say that I've been recently floored by the caliber of service of either Delta Airlines or Marriott hotels, two brands cited as clients (nor was it ever exceptional at Shake Shack.

The most glaring flaw in this entire espionage narrative boils down to a basic misunderstanding of human anatomy. Phimosis is a structural, physical restriction. Circumcision fixes it; Viagra does not. In fact, prescribing a vasodilator for severe phimosis only amplifies the pain and tension.
There is a striking geopolitical analogy here. The great powers of that era attempted to micro-manage and manipulate a world that was otherwise functioning, driving us directly into the modern chaos we see across the Middle East today. Instead of obsession over control, ideological supremacy, and continuous fighting over petty distinctions of race, religion, class, and caste, imagine what would have happened if that energy had been directed toward global science, health, and actual problem-solving.
Addressing any crisis—whether human anatomy or international diplomacy—requires treating the actual structural reality, not applying aggressive, surface-level quick fixes that only worsen the underlying tension.

It's important to remember that there are two forces at work here, not one. 

The first and probably the most powerful is the slow but steady takeover of academic power by corporations. This takeover can't be easily mapped onto conservative or liberal--it is much better described as corporatization or neoliberal, and its purpose is just money, money, money. This is the force that wants to require fewer credits to graduate and disregards the idea of a liberal education in the mode of a Cardinal Newman--an education that aims to create good citizens, not just capable workers. 

The second force is the conservatism that disdains and devalues any kind of academic investigation of gender, race or class. These folks are on board with the neoliberals at this point, because they see that cutting back on core classes is an opportunity to attack their favorite political targets. 

When you put these two forces together, and add some AI into the mix, you've got an actual crisis in higher education. I teach in the humanities at a community college and it literally feels to me like the academic world I knew is falling away. I think there are real opportunities here for humanities scholars to circle our wagons and organize. I see this in programs like The Great Questions Foundation here in Texas and at other programs nationwide. It's not the conservative "civics" centers, it's organizations that are working to consolidate some requirements in humanities, where they should still be.

I saw a man who had his young daughter go to his car and asked him if he would take our family with him.  It was nearly 98 degrees in the shade and he gave us a ride.  

I started a conversation with him and found out he was from Poland…I was in the back seat and we were speaking about famous poets and writers and he said “I’m quite surprised because you’re an American and you know the very best.”  Hmm.  I then asked him if he knows or read Bruno Schulz?  His head snapped back and he looked intently at me and then started speaking to himself in Polish. Just so happens that 16 years before I became obsessed with him and all of his work, art, and his extraordinary tragic life.  He told me that no person outside of his country knew him and he was so very moved.  

Words move. Poetry moves.  People and lands merge in love and it was the best ride I ever had.  Bruno is a rare treasure from Poland.  I first read everything in German but it’s available in English.  Awesome human being.  And great teacher.

If anyone wants to know how to pronounce the names of Irish places, look to the spelling of the Irish words which for Dunguaire would be Dún Guaire.

Going to teanglann, an online Irish dictionary, if you look up the word dún you see it means fort and you can listen to three native Irish speakers say it in their regional dialect (Connaught, Munster and Ulster). 

By the way, any Irish word with the fada (accent) is elongated, so i you see a fada on a vowel it's a long sound. The word fada actually means long. 

Dún has a fada, Guaire does not. You can also listen to the three speakers pronounce guaire on teanglann. Guaire means both "bristle" and "sand barrier at the river mouth." 

Irish places names in their English equivalent make no sense whatsoever. But many names of Irish places in their original Irish often make a lot of sense.

Mr. Barry, please consider doing a story about the revival of the Irish language that is happening now on the island. President Catherine Connolly is centering it in her administration. Kneecap is very popular. Irish language film is doing well too. Poems are being written in Irish and about Irish. 

And it is all happening concurrently with a rewilding of the island, reclaiming more of the the land as temperate rainforest. I do not believe it is a coincidence that the language and the land are healing together.

Go raibh maith agat.

It was an immensely fertile time in New York City, before the cultural retrenchment of the Reagan years and critics such as Samuel Lipman. We also lost much of the presence created by the old Museum of the American Indian and the Huntington Free Library. comments.name: David Robertson
comments.body: There's a nude descending a staircase somewhere in this novel, as in Marcel Duchamp's identically named painting of 1912. There's that same Cubist and Futurist deconstruction of motion into endless sequences, the same shifting and changing viewpoints, the same distortions of linear time. Great stuff for the early 20th century, but it now sounds a little outdated. "If you live long enough, you become a migrant from another timeline," a character declares in this novel, using the buzzword "timeline" from the business and science of the 1950s and 1960s. How better written this sentence would have been had the author simply stopped writing after the word "migrant." Perhaps this novel itself is an exit party of the avant-garde and the experimental, and that party's long over.
